doc.title: Dick Spottswood interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 13, 2023

title: Defining the blues and the cowboy beat of Bob Wills
summary: He argues Bob Wills is a blues singer, links Wills to southwestern jazz bands, Moten, Basie and Charlie Christian, and mentions Frank Driggs.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: I’m forming a question here because it fascinates me, and I don’t know if you can do this, but if you were at a cocktail party and someone asks you, “Well what is the blues anyway” what’s the first thing that you want to say about it, if you want to try and bother?

I don’t know, I mean it’s not a word that requires a precise definition. I mean it’s not like something that would be in a scientific or mathematical appraisal. If it’s art it’s flexible. I mean isn’t Bob Wills a pretty good blues singer? So what is he singing, country? Maybe. Western? Well is he singing the blues? I mean his favorite singer was Bessie Smith or does his being white disqualify it? I’m not saying yes or no to that but there’s the question. Right? If you listen to some of Bob Wills’ records, especially the pre-War ones, they’re out swinging a lot of those big bands out of New York and Chicago because they’ve got that cowboy beat.

They danced like people did in the southwest, you know like those wonderful Bennie Moten records throughout the twenties and early thirties. Like those few location recordings that were made by the Basie band right after it came out of Kansas City into Chicago and to New York. And some of those other territory bands, I can’t think of names right off the hand, but when you could hear other music from the southwest you’re hearing Charlie Christian, you’re hearing Bob Wills, you’re hearing Milton Brown, you’re hearing Doug [inaudible], you’re hearing Hershel Evans. All of those people with a record like — there’s a wonderful photo in a Bob Wills book of Bob and Henry Allen and Tommy Duncan and one or two other jazz people. Maybe it was Higginbotham or © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

somebody, all sitting around the table having drinks together in the forties. Those musicians knew each other. They didn’t have those problems. The music was the music and if you heard a Bob Wills record without singing you wouldn’t think it was a white band. Their version of “White Heat” really skunks the Jimmie Lunceford version.
Yike. You know you and I could talk for about four days solid I think. I want to read —
I think Frank Driggs would probably hit me across the head if he heard all of this, but I never had that discussion with Frank.
When he discussed southwestern music he never brought into it the western sweet bands and I think they’re a big part of that equation and I think the influence went both ways.
